title: Industrial Sector Performance Index
description: Industrial Sector Performance Index offers an outlook for manufacturing and industrial sectors performance based on key indicators such as PMI, energy requirements, capacity utilisation, and production quantity of key raw materials.…

qna.question: What is the Industrial Sector Performance Index?
qna.answer: Industrial Sector Performance Index offers an outlook for manufacturing and industrial sectors performance based on key indicators such as PMI, energy requirements, capacity utilisation, and production quantity of key raw materials. Industrial Sector Performance Index indicates the demand for goods, production trends, and also provides a near to medium term outlook, which is crucial for assessing investment activity by industries and production trends in the economy. The index captures demand and supply side fluctuations, impact of domestic and global policy changes such as tax reforms, industrial policies and seasonal variations in the industry and their impact on employment and growth.

qna.question: What are its components?
qna.answer: The index covers diverse economic parameters, covering both demand and supply side factors. We have assigned appropriate weights to each of these indicators to capture the trends and outlook of the industrial sector activities.

qna.question: How to use the Industrial Sector Performance Index for better financial decision-making?
qna.answer: The industrial sector is a bellwether for economic conditions and plays a pivotal role in the well-being of a nation's population, impacting everything from employment to income levels. Understanding the performance of this sector allows individuals and businesses to develop robust, adaptive financial strategies that are well-equipped to capitalise on emerging opportunities.

index_meta.phase_summary: A transitory slowdown in the industrial sector occurs when the performance and output of industries involved in manufacturing, production, and related activities start to move towards slowdown.
index_meta.success_rate_description: A measure of how well the Industrial Sector Performance Index has historically predicted the Industrial sector GVA growth

interpretation.title: 0-25 = Recession
interpretation.description: If the index drops below 25 and continues to remain beneath this level for two consecutive quarters, it indicates the services sector has entered into a recessionary phase.

interpretation.title: 25-50 = Weak Recovery / Sharp Slowdown
interpretation.description: Following a recession, the index level typically rises from 25 and progresses towards 50.If the index level stays between this range for several months, it signifies the industrial sector is slowly recovering.A sharp slowdown phase often precedes a recession. If the index level shifts towards 25 from 50, it indicates a sharp slowdown in the industrial sector.

interpretation.title: 50-75 = Strong Recovery / Transitory Slowdown
interpretation.description: If the index rebounds from 50 and remains between 50 and 75, with upward direction, then there is a strong recovery in the industrial sector.However, if the repo rate remains high, then the direction of the index may fluctuate from 50 to 75, or from 75 to 50, reflecting a transitory slowdown.

interpretation.title: 75-100 = Growth
interpretation.description: If the index crosses 75 and consistently remains above this level, it indicates the industrial sector has entered into a growth phase.

recent_updates: The HSBC Manufacturing PMI rose to 55.1 in September 2026 from 52.8 in August, marking the strongest improvement in seven months. New orders grew at the fastest pace in seven months, factory hiring resumed, and business confidence rose to a four-month high.

Industrial output (IIP) grew 8.0% year-on-year in August 2026, up from 7.4% in July, with manufacturing growing 9.0% and electricity 12.3%. Capital goods (16.9%) and intermediate goods (13.7%) led the use-based categories, pointing to strong investment demand, while mining contracted 5.6%.

Manufacturing capacity utilisation stood at 74.6% in Q1 FY27 (76.3% on a seasonally adjusted basis), higher than 74.1% a year earlier, according to the RBI's OBICUS survey. New orders grew 14.3% year-on-year, indicating healthy demand ahead.

Core sector growth moderated to 4.8% year-on-year in August 2026 from 5.0% in July. Cement (12.5%) and electricity (11.6%) grew strongly, while fertilisers (-12.4%), natural gas (-4.9%), coal (-3.8%) and crude oil (-3.6%) contracted, highlighting continued weakness in the energy segment.
near_term_outlook: India's industrial sector is expected to maintain strong growth in FY27, supported by public capital spending, rising order books and investment-led demand in capital and intermediate goods.
We expect the Manufacturing PMI to remain in the 54–56 range over the coming months, supported by stronger new orders and export demand.
Capacity utilisation is expected to remain around 75–77% on a seasonally adjusted basis, supporting a gradual pickup in private-sector investment.

Rising input costs, with crude oil above USD 100 per barrel, and the October repo rate hike pose the main risks. Weakness in mining, coal and fertilisers is likely to keep industrial growth uneven across sectors.

historical_events.title: Rise of Protectionism around the World: US and EU Elections
historical_events.description: The EU and the US are India’s largest trading partners and a key source of FDI and Exports. Donald Trump’s victory in the 2024 elections and his subsequent announcement of reciprocal tariffs on trading partners reignited the concerns around protectionist policies as a means. European Parliament (EP) is the EU’s directly elected legislative body, with 720 members (MEPs) representing 27 member states. Elections occur every five years.
historical_events.origin: Donald Trump aims to reduce the US trade deficits with multiple trading partners by making imports more expensive and encouraging domestic production. His administration argues that tariffs protect US industries from foreign competition, particularly China, act as a source of revenue and serve as negotiation leverage to address non-trade issues. EU Parliamentary elections in 2024 took place in a context of an ongoing war in Ukraine, energy security concerns, populism, and debates on migration and climate policy. The elections saw significant gains for parties advocating nationalist and protectionist policies.

impacts.title: Exports Reduction:
impacts.description: A rise in protectionism could lead to a decline in Indian exports to these regions. Tariffs directly raise costs for Indian exports in key sectors like automobiles, electronics, steel, and textiles. For example, up to $5 bn of auto and electronics exports to the US could be affected.

impacts.title: Job Losses:
impacts.description: Higher compliance costs and tariffs threaten the competitiveness of India’s exports, affecting output and job creation, especially for MSMEs, which are major employment generators.

historical_events.title: Production Linked Incentive Scheme 2.0 and Renewable Energy Push
historical_events.description: The Production Linked Incentive Scheme provides financial incentives to companies based on incremental sales from products manufactured in domestic units. It aims to boost domestic manufacturing, enhance export capabilities, and reduce import dependence. It was launched in March 2020 and expanded to include 14 critical industries in 2023 and 2024. The National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM), launched in Jan 2023, aims to position India as a global leader in green hydrogen production, utilisation, and export.
historical_events.origin: The PLI scheme covers 14 key sectors: automobiles, electronic systems, pharmaceuticals, textiles, food processing, aviation, chemicals, metals and mining, renewable energy, telecom, medical devices, drones, and white goods.  Under this scheme, both domestic and foreign companies receive financial rewards for manufacturing in India, calculated as a percentage of their revenue over up to five years. NGHM emerged from India’s commitment to net-zero emissions by 2070 and reducing the carbon intensity of its GDP by 45% by 2030. It also seeks to reduce fossil fuel imports, address energy security, decarbonization, and the shift to renewable energy to achieve climate goals

impacts.title: Economic Impact of PLI:
impacts.description: The PLI scheme has stimulated investments in high-tech industries like electronics, automotive, and pharmaceuticals, fostering innovation and R&D activities. As of Aug '24, investment of ₹1.46 lakh cr has been realised, resulting in incremental production of over ₹12.50 lakh cr, employment generation of over 9.5 lakhs, and exports surpassing ₹4 lakh cr.

impacts.title: The economic impact of NGHM:
impacts.description: It is projected to exceed ₹8 lakh crore worth of investments, job creation of over 6 lakhs throughout the value chain, and a reduction in fossil fuel imports by over ₹1 lakh crore by 2030. Additionally, the mission is expected to avert nearly 50 MMT of annual greenhouse gas emissions, contributing significantly to India's climate goals.

historical_events.title: Russia - Ukraine War
historical_events.description: The Russia-Ukraine War, escalating significantly with Russia’s military intervention in Ukraine on February 24, 2022, was a major geopolitical conflict that has caused widespread international concern and economic repercussions. It marks a severe intensification of the long-standing tensions between Russia and Ukraine.
historical_events.origin: The conflict has its roots in historical, political, and cultural disputes, intensifying with Ukraine's move towards European integration and away from the Russian sphere of influence. The situation escalated dramatically with Russia's military intervention in Ukraine, leading to severe geopolitical tensions and international sanctions against Russia affecting global politics, economies, and supply chains.

impacts.title: Disruption in Energy Markets:
impacts.description: One of the most immediate impacts of the war was the disruption in global energy markets. Russia is a major exporter of oil and natural gas, and the conflict led to significant fluctuations in global oil prices. The Indian Basket of crude oil, which was priced at $89.4 per barrel on February 1, 2022, witnessed a sharp increase, peaking at $128.2 per barrel on March 10, 2022 due to the outbreak of the conflict.

impacts.title: Supply Chain and Trade Disruptions:
impacts.description: The conflict caused major disruptions in global supply chains and trade. The closure of Black Sea ports, a vital route for grain and oil shipments, and sanctions against Russia, impacted the transportation and availability of various commodities and goods.

impacts.title: Economic Sanctions and their Impact:
impacts.description: The extensive sanctions imposed on Russia by Western countries had significant economic repercussions, not only for Russia but also for countries with strong economic ties to it. These sanctions affected sectors like banking, technology, and energy, and had ripple effects on the global economy.

historical_events.title: Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme
historical_events.description: The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme, notified by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) on April 16, 2021, was a strategic initiative by the Indian government to encourage domestic manufacturing and increase exports. This scheme was part of a broader national effort to position India as a global manufacturing hub.
historical_events.origin: Launched in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, the PLI scheme aimed to attract investments in key sectors and cutting-edge technology; ensure efficiency and bring economies of size and scale in the manufacturing sector and make Indian companies and manufacturers globally competitive. It was designed to incentivise companies to scale up their production and enhance India’s manufacturing capabilities, thereby reducing dependence on imports.

impacts.title: Investment Attraction:
impacts.description: The PLI scheme was successful in attracting significant investments across various sectors. For example, in the electronics sector, major global players like Samsung and Apple’s suppliers committed to increasing their production capacities in India. The scheme Over ₹ 95,000 Crores of investment reported till September 2023, which has led to production/sales of ₹ 7.80 Lakh crores and employment generation (direct & indirect) of over 6.4 lakh.

impacts.title: Boost in Manufacturing Output:
impacts.description: The scheme was projected to significantly elevate manufacturing output in targeted sectors. There has been a value addition of 20% in mobile manufacturing within a period of 3 years. Of the $ 101 billion total electronics production in FY2023, smartphones constitute $ 44 billion, including $ 11.1 billion as exports.

impacts.title: Sector-Specific Impacts:
impacts.description: Each sector under the PLI scheme had specific targets and incentives. For example, in the pharmaceutical sector, the scheme was designed to encourage the production of high-value products and reduce dependency on imports of critical drugs. There has been a significant reduction in imports of raw materials in the Pharma sector. Unique intermediate materials and bulk drugs are being manufactured in India including Penicillin-G, and transfer of technology has happened in manufacturing of Medical Devices such as CT scan, MRI etc. Similarly, in the Telecom sector import substitution of 60% has been achieved, and India has become almost self–reliant in Antennae, GPON (Gigabit Passive Optical Network) & CPE (Customer Premises Equipment). Drones sector has seen a 7 times jump in turnover, which consists of all MSME Startups. Under the PLI Scheme for Food Processing, sourcing of raw materials from India has seen significant increase which has positively impacted income of Indian farmers and MSMEs.

historical_events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic and Lockdown
historical_events.description: The COVID-19 pandemic, a global health crisis caused by the novel coronavirus, began affecting India significantly from March 2020. Characterised by widespread infections, lockdowns, and public health emergencies, the pandemic has had profound implications on the Indian economy and society. According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), COVID-19 caused 5,33,318 deaths as of December 19, 2023.
historical_events.origin: First identified in December 2019 in Wuhan, Hubei, China, the COVID-19 virus transmitted rapidly across the globe and affected several people within a month. The World Health Organisation (WHO) declared it a pandemic in March 2020. India, with its large population and high population density, faced significant challenges in controlling the spread of the virus. Considering the seriousness of the disease, and to control the transmission of COVID-19, the central government announced a 21-day nationwide lockdown in March 2020 (March 25, 2020 to April 14, 2020). There have been three more lockdown phases in succession. During lockdowns many industries, academic institutes, markets, as well as public gatherings were shut down severely disrupting the overall economic activities.

impacts.title: Supply Chain Disruptions:
impacts.description: The pandemic caused severe disruptions in global and domestic supply chains. In India, the manufacturing sector, which often relies on just-in-time supply chains, faced acute challenges due to halted imports and exports. For instance, the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) for manufacturing, which is a measure of the health of the manufacturing sector, plummeted to an all-time low of 27.4 in April 2020, indicating a significant contraction in manufacturing activities.

impacts.title: Labour Shortages:
impacts.description: Labour shortages were another critical impact of the pandemic and lockdowns. With the imposition of movement restrictions, migrant workers, a significant part of the workforce in various industries, were unable to return to their workplaces. This led to a substantial reduction in available labour, particularly affecting sectors like construction and textiles.

impacts.title: Halt in Manufacturing Activities:
impacts.description: Manufacturing activities came to a near standstill during the initial phase of the lockdown. Industries such as automotive, textiles, and electronics faced significant operational challenges and revenue losses. The automotive sector, for example, saw zero domestic sales in April 2020 for the first time in history.

impacts.title: Acceleration of Automation and Digital Transformation:
impacts.description: A notable long-term impact of the pandemic has been the accelerated adoption of automation and digital technologies. To cope with labour shortages and adapt to the new normal, many industries accelerated their digital transformation initiatives. For instance, there was a marked increase in the adoption of e-commerce, digital payments, and remote working technologies across various sectors.

impacts.title: Economic Contraction and Recovery:
impacts.description: The Indian economy contracted sharply due to the pandemic, with GDP shrinking by 23.37% in Q1FY2020 year-on-year (YoY). However, following the initial shock, signs of economic recovery began to emerge, driven by gradual relaxations in lockdowns and the government's stimulus measures.

historical_events.title: Implementation of GST
historical_events.description: On July 1, 2017, India underwent a major tax reform with the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST), marking a significant milestone in the country's taxation history. GST was introduced as a comprehensive indirect tax on the manufacture, sale, and consumption of goods and services throughout India, replacing multiple cascading taxes levied by the central and state governments.
historical_events.origin: The move towards GST was driven by the need to unify the country's fragmented tax system into a single, transparent, and efficient tax regime. Prior to GST, India had a complex tax structure with various state and central taxes, leading to inefficiencies and tax-on-tax (cascading effect). The implementation of GST aimed to simplify this system, broaden the tax base, and create a common market across states, thereby boosting ease of doing business and overall economic growth.

impacts.title: Unified Common National Market:
impacts.description: GST replaced multiple state and central taxes with a single tax system, thereby eliminating the barriers to inter-state trade and commerce. This unification created a seamless national market, facilitating easier movement and supply of goods across state borders.

impacts.title: Reduction of Cascading Tax Effect:
impacts.description: One of the primary achievements of GST was the elimination of the cascading effect of taxes. By allowing the set-off of prior-stage taxes, GST reduced the overall tax burden on goods and services, potentially lowering prices for consumers and increasing the competitiveness of Indian products.

impacts.title: Enhanced Supply Chain Efficiency:
impacts.description: With the removal of inter-state checkpoints and a more streamlined tax process, GST significantly improved supply chain efficiency. This was particularly evident in sectors like logistics and warehousing, where reduced transit times and lower costs were observed.

impacts.title: Tax Collection and Compliance:
impacts.description: The GST regime, being technology-driven, brought in greater transparency and compliance. In FY2019, the total GST collection amounted to approximately ₹ 11.77 Lakh Crores, indicating a healthy increase in tax compliance and revenue generation.

impacts.title: Impact on Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) and Other Sectors:
impacts.description: While GST provided a more structured tax framework, its implementation posed challenges for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) and certain sectors. These entities had to navigate the complexities of the new system, adapt to the technological requirements, and contend with initial operational hurdles.

historical_events.title: Demonetisation
historical_events.description: Demonetisation, announced on November 8, 2016, was a significant decision by the Indian government to withdraw the legal tender character of the Specified Bank Notes (SBNs), involving the high-value currency notes (₹ 500 and ₹ 1,000) from circulation. It represented a drastic step by the government in its fight to curb black money, counterfeit currency and corruption.
historical_events.origin: The primary objective behind this decision was to curb black money, counterfeit currency, and corruption. The move was also aimed at promoting digital financial transactions and bringing more of the informal economy into the formal sector. The government announced this decision abruptly, leading to widespread and immediate impact across the country.

impacts.title: Disruption in the Manufacturing Sector:
impacts.description: Demonetisation led to immediate disruptions in the manufacturing sector. The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) in manufacturing, which measures manufacturing output, saw a sharp decline, and registered a growth of just 0.6% in December 2016, as compared to 4.8% in October 2016.

impacts.title: Effect on Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs):
impacts.description: The impact was particularly severe on Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) which relied heavily on cash transactions. Many of these businesses experienced a significant slowdown in their operations due to liquidity constraints.

impacts.title: Short-term Economic Slowdown:
impacts.description: The GDP growth rate slowed down to 8.58% in Q3FY2016, from 9.67% in Q2FY2016. This slowdown was a direct consequence of reduced consumer spending and a disruption in business activities.

impacts.title: Increase in Digital Transactions:
impacts.description: One positive outcome was a significant increase in digital transactions. The volume of electronic payment systems, such as NEFT and mobile wallets, saw a substantial rise post-demonetisation. For instance, mobile banking transactions experienced significant growth, rising from 78.12 million in October 2016, to 110.64 million in December 2016. The upward trend continued with a surge to 206.5 million by December 2017, ultimately surpassing 1,080 million in November 2023.

impacts.title: Impact on Banking and Financial Sector:
impacts.description: The banking sector saw an influx of deposits as people queued to deposit old currency notes. As per an internal study by the Reserve Bank of India, excess deposits in banks during the 50 days of demonetisation worked out to ₹ 4 trillion. This temporary surge in bank deposits provided banks with more liquidity, which could potentially be leveraged for lending and investment purposes in the long run.

historical_events.title: Make in India Initiative
historical_events.description: The Make in India initiative, launched on September 25, 2014, was a significant campaign by the Indian government aimed at transforming India into a global manufacturing hub. It is one of the unique 'Vocal for Local' initiatives that promoted India's manufacturing domain to the world. It sought to encourage both national and international companies to manufacture their products in India.
historical_events.origin: This initiative was launched against the backdrop of a need to stimulate the Indian economy, create large-scale job opportunities, attract foreign investment, foster innovation, and build best-in-class infrastructure. It targeted key sectors of the economy, emphasising ease of doing business, faster approvals, and modernising India’s industrial infrastructure. The 'Make in India' initiative has significant achievements and presently focuses on 27 sectors under Make in India 2.0.

impacts.title: Attraction of Foreign Direct Investment:
impacts.description: Make in India led to a notable increase in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). For instance, FDI inflows in FY2016 reached about $ 55.46 billion, a significant increase from $ 45.15 billion in FY2015. This trend was particularly evident in sectors highlighted by the initiative, such as defence, electronics, and automotive.

impacts.title: Growth in Key Manufacturing Sectors:
impacts.description: Specific manufacturing sectors saw substantial growth due to this initiative. The automotive sector, for example, experienced a boost in both production and export, with companies such as Hyundai and Suzuki expanding their manufacturing capacities in India. Similarly, the electronics manufacturing sector witnessed an increase, with companies such as Samsung and Foxconn announcing large investments in Indian operations.

impacts.title: Technology Transfer and Development:
impacts.description: The initiative encouraged technology transfer and fostered innovation in various sectors. For instance, in the defence sector, the initiative paved the way for collaborations between Indian companies and global defence manufacturers, leading to the transfer of technology and development of indigenous defence products.

impacts.title: Job Creation:
impacts.description: One of the primary goals of Make in India was to create employment. While exact figures vary, the initiative contributed to job creation in various sectors through both direct and indirect employment opportunities, particularly in the manufacturing and service sectors linked to manufacturing.

impacts.title: Global Perception:
impacts.description: Make in India played a pivotal role in improving the global perception of India as a manufacturing destination. The initiative's emphasis on policy reforms and infrastructure development enhanced investor confidence, positioning India more favourably in the global economic landscape.

historical_events.title: National Manufacturing Policy
historical_events.description: The National Manufacturing Policy (NMP), implemented on November 4, 2011, was an ambitious initiative by the Indian government to revitalise the country's manufacturing sector. Its primary goal was to increase the sector's contribution to the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and create massive employment opportunities.
historical_events.origin: The policy was introduced in the context of India's burgeoning economy, with an emphasis on shifting the economic focus from agriculture and services to manufacturing. The aim was to elevate the manufacturing sector's share in the GDP to 25% by 2022, a significant increase from the 16% it held at the time of the policy's inception.

impacts.title: Establishment of Manufacturing Zones:
impacts.description: A key element of the NMP was the establishment of National Investment and Manufacturing Zones (NIMZs). These zones were conceived as integrated industrial townships with state-of-the-art infrastructure, aimed at promoting world-class manufacturing activities.

impacts.title: Infrastructure Development:
impacts.description: The policy led to an enhanced focus on infrastructure development, crucial for the growth of the manufacturing sector. This included improvements in transportation, power supply, and technology, all of which are essential for efficient manufacturing operations.

impacts.title: Business Regulation Reforms:
impacts.description: NMP initiated significant reforms in business regulations, aimed at simplifying and streamlining processes. This included reducing the bureaucratic hurdles for starting and operating a manufacturing business, thereby creating a more conducive environment for both domestic and foreign investors.

impacts.title: Manufacturing GDP Contribution:
impacts.description: While the target was to raise the manufacturing sector's contribution to 25% of GDP by 2022, the increase in the years following the policy was negligible. By FY2023, the manufacturing sector's contribution to GDP remained at around 18%, compared to 17% in 2012.

impacts.title: Employment Opportunities:
impacts.description: One of the policy's objectives was to create 100 million additional jobs in the manufacturing sector by 2022. In the initial years following the policy, there was an increase in employment, although the exact figures varied across different regions and sectors.

historical_events.title: Special Economic Zones (SEZ) Act
historical_events.description: The Special Economic Zones (SEZ) Act, enacted on June 23, 2005, was a pivotal step by the Indian government aimed at invigorating export-oriented growth. This legislation established a legal framework for the creation and operation of SEZs, designed to enhance economic activities, particularly in the export sector.
historical_events.origin: Introduced to improve upon the limitations of earlier export processing zones, the Special Economic Zones (SEZ) Act's objectives were to attract foreign investment, boost exports, and enhance the manufacturing sector's competitiveness through a more liberal and investor-friendly environment.

impacts.title: Manufacturing Boost and Export Growth:
impacts.description: Following the enactment of the SEZ Act, there was a significant uptick in manufacturing activities within these zones. SEZs have emerged as an important contributor to India's exports, which nearly doubled to about ₹ 66,638 Crores by FY2008, highlighting the effectiveness of SEZs in enhancing India's export capabilities. Total exports from these zones stood at $ 155.8 billion in FY2023 including $ 61.6 billion of merchandise and $ 94.2 billion of service exports.

impacts.title: Sectoral Advancements:
impacts.description: Sectors such as textiles, pharmaceuticals, and electronics within SEZs experienced notable growth in this period. The pharmaceutical sector, in particular, saw a significant rise in exports, reflecting the targeted impact of the SEZs in key industries.

impacts.title: Attracting Foreign Direct Investment:
impacts.description: The initial years post-SEZ Act saw a surge in foreign direct investment, demonstrating growing global investor confidence in India's manufacturing and export sectors within SEZs.

impacts.title: Job Creation:
impacts.description: Employment in SEZs expanded substantially, contributing to both skilled and unskilled workforce growth in the manufacturing sector. This increase in employment was a direct result of the enhanced industrial activity in SEZs.

historical_events.title: New Industrial Policy
historical_events.description: Introduced on July 24, 1991, the new industrial policy represented a radical shift from the previously restrictive industrial regulations that had governed the Indian manufacturing sector for decades. The overarching aim was to increase efficiency and competitiveness in the industrial sector, attract foreign investment, and integrate the Indian economy with the global market.
historical_events.origin: In July 1991, India was at a crucial juncture, grappling with a severe economic crisis. The nation faced a daunting balance of payments predicament, with foreign exchange reserves plunging to levels that could barely cover a few weeks of imports. This dire situation prompted the government to initiate a series of radical economic reforms, including the New Industrial Policy.

impacts.title: Growth in Manufacturing Output:
impacts.description: Post-reform, the manufacturing sector witnessed substantial growth. The average annual growth rate of the manufacturing sector increased from around 5% during the 1980s to approximately 7% between 1992 and 1996. This marked a clear uptick in industrial activity and output.

impacts.title: Diversification of Industries:
impacts.description: The policy fostered diversification within the manufacturing sector. Previously constrained sectors such as textiles, automobiles, and electronics saw significant expansion and diversification, reflecting a more dynamic industrial base.

impacts.title: Challenges and Modernisation:
impacts.description: The initial years post-liberalisation saw some industries struggling to adapt, leading to a phase of consolidation and modernisation. Investments in technology and quality upgradation became pivotal for survival in the new market dynamics.

impacts.title: Increase in Foreign Investment:
impacts.description: The period following the New Industrial Policy saw a marked increase in foreign investment in manufacturing, contributing to technology transfer and capital inflow. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) to India in the manufacturing sector, which was negligible pre-1991, surged significantly, representing as much as 83% of total FDI to India in 1995.

impacts.title: Global Integration and Exports:
impacts.description: The policy facilitated greater integration of the Indian manufacturing sector with the global economy. Exports from the manufacturing sector grew from $ 13.245 billion in FY1992 to $ 23.775 billion, with a 12% CAGR, making Indian products more competitive internationally.

insights.label: Identifying Trends in Key Sub-sectors:
insights.definition: By analysing trends in sub-sectors such as production trends in manufacturing, credit demand and capacity utilisation, investors can gauge business conditions. For instance, a surge in manufacturing output might suggest an opportune moment to invest in related stocks or sector-specific mutual funds. A consistent increase in IIP might signal a growing industrial activity, suggesting a potentially favourable time to invest in industrial raw material stocks.

insights.label: Demand Forecasting in the Industry:
insights.definition: Indicators such as sale of consumer durables, non-durables, and energy requirements shed light on domestic consumer demand for the manufactured products, aiding in the adjustment of spending and savings strategies, particularly during economic downturns.

insights.label: Predictive Employment Trends:
insights.definition: Observing trends in the industrial sector offers a predictive view of job market stability. This is crucial for individuals employed in this sector to plan for financial security and emergency savings. For example, steady growth in production enhances the prospects for job creation and stability in the manufacturing industry and also indicates a stable investment environment for employees in this sector.

insights.label: Policy Changes and Tax Reforms Impact:
insights.definition: Monitoring shifts in policy and tax reforms related to the industrial sector is essential to strategically align the investments to either mitigate risks or leverage new opportunities that arise from these economic policy shifts.
